lessons.title: Lowest Common Ancestor
lessons.objective: Find the lowest common ancestor of two nodes in a binary tree using postorder DFS, and optimise to O(h) for BSTs by exploiting the BST invariant.
concepts: LCA definition: deepest node that is an ancestor of both p and q
Ancestor definition: a node is its own ancestor (LeetCode convention)
General binary tree LCA: postorder DFS returning node or null
Three cases: p and q in different subtrees, one is ancestor of other, neither found
BST LCA: exploit invariant to go left or right without full traversal
General tree: O(n) time O(h) space
BST: O(h) time O(h) space
LCA applications: distance between nodes, path queries
lessons.explanation: The Lowest Common Ancestor (LCA) of two nodes p and q is the deepest node in the tree that has both p and q as descendants, where a node is considered a descendant of itself. For a general binary tree, the postorder DFS approach: if the current node is null, return null. If the current node is p or q, return it (it is either the LCA or part of the path to LCA). Recurse on both children. If both return non-null, the current node is the LCA (p is in one subtree, q in the other). If only one returns non-null, return that non-null result (both nodes are in the same subtree, and the returned node is the LCA). For a BST, the LCA is the split point where p and q diverge. If both p and q are less than root, LCA is in the left subtree. If both are greater, LCA is in the right subtree. If one is on each side (or one equals root), root is the LCA. This BST approach is O(h) because it traverses a single path from root to LCA without visiting all nodes.
lessons.analogy: LCA in a binary tree is like finding the nearest common postal hub for two delivery addresses. You start at the central depot (root) and trace both addresses down the network. The last hub where both routes share the same building (before splitting into different branches) is the LCA. For a BST, the hub structure is sorted, so you can navigate directly without checking every hub.

code_example.explanation: The general tree LCA works because when both left and right return non-null, it means p was found in one subtree and q in the other — so the current node is exactly where the paths to p and q diverge, making it the LCA. When only one side returns non-null, both nodes are in the same subtree and the answer has already been determined deeper in the recursion.

common_mistakes: Returning root as LCA before recursing when root equals p or q, missing the case where one node is an ancestor of the other — returning immediately when root is p or q is correct in LeetCode's convention because p is an ancestor of itself; if p is an ancestor of q, p is the LCA
Not handling the case where one node does not exist in the tree — the standard LCA algorithm assumes both p and q exist; if either might not exist, add a found_p and found_q flag
Using the BST LCA on a general binary tree — BST LCA exploits sorted structure; it gives wrong answers on trees where the BST property does not hold
lessons.interview_relevance: Lowest Common Ancestor of a Binary Tree (#236) and LCA of a BST (#235) are both Blind 75. They are asked at every major company. The BST variant is the warm-up; the general tree variant is the main problem. Being able to articulate why the general tree solution returns node when both subtrees are non-null is the key explanatory step interviewers listen for.

flashcards.front: What is the LCA (Lowest Common Ancestor) of two nodes p and q?
flashcards.back: The deepest node in the tree that has both p and q as descendants, where a node is considered a descendant of itself (LeetCode convention).

flashcards.front: General binary tree LCA: what does the helper return?
flashcards.back: null if neither p nor q found in the subtree. The node itself if it is p or q. The LCA node if both p and q are found in different subtrees.

flashcards.front: Why does returning root when both left and right are non-null give the LCA?
flashcards.back: It means p was found in one subtree and q in the other. The current node is exactly where their paths diverge upward — making it the deepest common ancestor.

flashcards.front: BST LCA: how does the BST invariant help?
flashcards.back: If both p and q are less than root → LCA is in left subtree. If both are greater → right subtree. If they straddle the root (or one equals root) → root IS the LCA.

flashcards.front: Time and space complexity: general tree LCA vs BST LCA?
flashcards.back: General: O(n) time, O(h) space. BST: O(h) time, O(h) space (or O(1) iteratively). BST is faster because it never visits off-path nodes.

flashcards.front: When is a node its own ancestor in LCA problems?
flashcards.back: Always, by LeetCode convention. If p is an ancestor of q, then p is the LCA. The algorithm correctly returns p immediately when root===p without needing to find q.

flashcards.front: How to compute distance between two nodes using LCA?
flashcards.back: distance(p, q) = depth(p) + depth(q) - 2 × depth(LCA). Find LCA first, then compute depths of p, q, and LCA from root.

theory_mcq.question: What is the definition of Lowest Common Ancestor (LCA), including the LeetCode convention that 'a node is its own ancestor'?
options: LCA is the root of the tree, always

The LCA of two nodes p and q is the DEEPEST node that is an ancestor of BOTH p and q — under LeetCode's convention that a node counts as its own ancestor, if p is an ancestor of q, then p itself is the LCA (not a higher node)
LCA is the node that lies exactly between p and q in value
LCA is always the parent of whichever of p or q is deeper

theory_mcq.question: In the general binary tree LCA, what do the three cases `left && right`, `left only`, and `right only` represent when the postorder DFS returns?
options: They indicate whether the tree is balanced, left-heavy, or right-heavy

`left && right` (both non-null): p and q are in DIFFERENT subtrees — current root is the split point and therefore the LCA; `left only`: both p and q were found entirely in the left subtree — propagate left upward; `right only`: both found in right subtree — propagate right upward; in all non-split cases, one of p or q may itself be the ancestor of the other
They indicate the depth of p and q relative to the current node
The three cases are used only for BSTs, not general binary trees
theory_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's code logic: `if (left && right) return root` handles the split-point case (LCA found); `return left || right` propagates whichever non-null value was returned upward for the case where one subtree contains both nodes (or one node is ancestor of the other).

logic_mcq.question: Trace `lowestCommonAncestor` on the tree [3,5,1,6,2,0,8] for LCA(5,1). What does the DFS return from the left subtree (rooted at 5), from the right subtree (rooted at 1), and what is the final LCA?
options: Left returns null, right returns node(1), LCA is node(1)

Left subtree (rooted at 5): root===p (5===5), returns node(5) immediately; Right subtree (rooted at 1): root===q (1===1), returns node(1) immediately; At root=3: left=node(5) AND right=node(1), both non-null → returns root=node(3); LCA = 3 — matching the lesson's exact trace
Left returns node(6), right returns node(8), LCA is root
The function always returns the root for any two nodes
logic_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's exact trace: 'left subtree (5): root===p -> return node(5); right subtree (1): root===q -> return node(1); left=node(5), right=node(1): both non-null -> return root=node(3); LCA = 3'.

logic_mcq.question: For BST LCA, the iterative version uses `while (curr)` with a split-point check. Why is the BST LCA O(h) while the general tree LCA is O(n)?
options: Both are O(n); the BST version is no faster

The BST invariant allows the algorithm to DECIDE which subtree to enter at each step using only value comparisons — if both p and q are less than current node, go left (discarding the right subtree entirely); if both greater, go right; otherwise the split point is found; this eliminates O(n) remaining nodes at each step (for a balanced BST) vs the general tree version which must SCAN both subtrees since there's no ordering guarantee
BST LCA is O(h) only when the tree has exactly two levels
The general tree LCA is O(n²); the lesson's O(n) claim is wrong
logic_mcq.explanation: The BST invariant enables elimination of one entire subtree at each decision point — identical to BST search's O(h) reasoning from M07 L8: at each node, comparing p.val and q.val against current.val determines definitively which side the LCA lies on, halving the remaining search space (for balanced trees) rather than requiring full traversal.

logic_mcq.question: In `lowestCommonAncestorBST`, the split condition is `return root` when neither of the 'both left' or 'both right' conditions holds. What FOUR distinct sub-cases does this single return statement handle?
options: It only handles the case where p.val === q.val

The split return fires when: (1) p.val < root.val AND q.val > root.val (p left, q right); (2) p.val > root.val AND q.val < root.val (p right, q left); (3) root.val === p.val (root IS p, and q is somewhere in subtrees); (4) root.val === q.val (root IS q, and p is somewhere in subtrees) — in all four cases, root is the deepest node where the paths to p and q diverge or meet
It handles only one case: when p and q are on opposite sides
It handles the case when root has no children
logic_mcq.explanation: The two explicit branches handle 'both on left' and 'both on right'; everything else — both values straddling root (either side), or root equaling one of the targets — falls through to `return root`, correctly identifying root as the LCA in all four remaining cases under LeetCode's own-ancestor convention.

syntax_mcq.question: In `lowestCommonAncestor`, why does `if (root === p || root === q) return root` use REFERENCE equality (`===`) rather than value equality (`root.val === p.val`)?
options: Reference equality is always faster than value equality

The problem provides actual NODE REFERENCES (not just values) for p and q — reference equality checks whether `root` is literally the SAME NODE OBJECT as p or q in memory, which correctly identifies the node regardless of whether duplicate values exist in the tree; using value equality could incorrectly match a DIFFERENT node with the same value as p or q
LeetCode requires reference equality for all tree problems
Reference equality compares both val and pointer simultaneously
syntax_mcq.explanation: LCA problems pass actual TreeNode references (not integer values) for p and q — reference equality (`===`) correctly identifies whether the current node IS p or q (same object in memory), even in trees with duplicate values where multiple nodes might share the same val; value-based comparison would produce false matches on duplicate-valued nodes.

lessons.title: Right Side View Of Tree
lessons.objective: Implement Right Side View using both BFS (last node per level) and DFS (track depth, first visit per depth from right), and understand when each approach is cleaner.
concepts: Right side view: rightmost visible node at each depth
BFS approach: last node dequeued at each level
DFS approach: right subtree first, track max depth seen
DFS: a node is visible if it is the first visited at its depth from the right
Depth tracking: pass current depth as parameter
result.length as proxy for max depth seen so far
Left side view: symmetric swap of right and left
Both approaches O(n) time O(n) space
lessons.explanation: The right side view returns the values of nodes that are visible when you look at the tree from the right side — exactly one node per level, the rightmost one. BFS approach: process level by level using the standard level-grouping pattern from Module 7. At each level, the last node dequeued is the rightmost. DFS approach: do a modified preorder where you visit the right child before the left child. Pass the current depth as a parameter. When you visit a node at depth d for the first time, it is the rightmost node at that depth (because you always go right first). Track this with result.length: if result.length equals the current depth, this is the first node at this depth, so add it. This DFS approach is elegant and avoids the explicit level-size tracking of BFS. Both are O(n) but the DFS uses the call stack while BFS uses a queue.
lessons.analogy: Right side view from DFS is like a photographer who always photographs the rightmost person in each row of a group photo by walking along the right side of the group and photographing the first new face they see at each height level. Walking right-first in DFS ensures the first face seen at each depth is always the rightmost.

code_example.explanation: The depth === result.length check works because result.length always equals the number of distinct depths already recorded. When we visit a node at depth d, if result.length is d, we have not yet recorded any node at depth d (since result has entries for depths 0..d-1). Since we visit the right subtree before the left, the first node we see at each depth is always the rightmost.

common_mistakes: Visiting left before right in the DFS approach — the right-first visit order is what guarantees the first node seen at each depth is the rightmost; swapping to left-first gives the left side view
Using depth >= result.length instead of depth === result.length — >= would add multiple nodes per depth level on revisits; === correctly adds only the first node seen at each depth
Not handling the empty tree case before starting BFS or DFS — both approaches should return [] immediately for a null root
lessons.interview_relevance: Binary Tree Right Side View (#199) is Blind 75. Interviewers follow up with 'can you do it without BFS?' — the DFS approach is the answer. Knowing both approaches and being able to explain the depth === result.length invariant for the DFS version demonstrates tree fluency beyond memorised solutions.
lessons.mini_challenge: Implement both rightSideViewBFS and rightSideViewDFS and verify they return the same result for [1,2,3,null,5,null,4]. Then solve Binary Tree Level Averages: for each level, return the average value of nodes at that level. Use BFS with level grouping. Then solve Find Largest Value in Each Tree Row (LeetCode #515): return the maximum value at each level. Both use the same BFS level-grouping pattern as right side view.

flashcards.front: Right Side View: BFS approach in one line?
flashcards.back: Level-order BFS. At each level, push the LAST dequeued node's value to result.

flashcards.front: Right Side View: DFS approach key insight?
flashcards.back: Visit RIGHT child before LEFT. Pass depth as parameter. When depth === result.length, this is the first (rightmost) node seen at this depth — push its value.

flashcards.front: Why does depth === result.length mean 'first node at this depth'?
flashcards.back: result.length equals the number of depths already recorded (0 to result.length-1). When depth equals result.length, depth d has not been recorded yet — this is the first node at that depth.

flashcards.front: How do you get Left Side View from the DFS solution?
flashcards.back: Swap the recursion order: visit LEFT child first, then RIGHT. Same depth === result.length check. Now the first node seen at each depth is the leftmost.

flashcards.front: BFS vs DFS for Right Side View: which is cleaner?
flashcards.back: BFS is more intuitive (last node per level). DFS is more concise — no queue or levelSize tracking needed, just depth parameter and result.length check.

flashcards.front: Space complexity of BFS vs DFS Right Side View?
flashcards.back: BFS: O(w) where w = max level width (up to O(n) for last level). DFS: O(h) for call stack. DFS is better for wide trees, BFS for very deep trees.

theory_mcq.question: In the DFS approach to right side view, why does `depth === result.length` correctly identify the FIRST node visited at each depth, which is also the RIGHTMOST visible node?
options: result.length tracks the number of nodes, not the depth

`result.length` equals the number of depths already recorded — when `depth === result.length`, this depth has NOT yet been recorded (result has `depth` entries for depths 0 to depth-1); since DFS visits the RIGHT subtree FIRST, the very first node encountered at any new depth is necessarily the rightmost node at that depth; `result.push(node.val)` records it, so subsequent visits to the same depth find `depth < result.length` and skip
The condition only works for trees where all nodes are on the right side
depth === result.length is always false; the approach uses depth === result.length - 1
theory_mcq.explanation: This is the key insight of the DFS approach: `result.length` grows by 1 each time a new depth is first visited; by visiting right BEFORE left, the first node reached at each new depth (triggering `depth === result.length`) is always the rightmost visible node at that depth — exactly what the right side view requires.

theory_mcq.question: When would you prefer the DFS approach over the BFS approach for right side view, and vice versa?
options: BFS is always preferable; DFS has no advantages here

BFS is more INTUITIVE for 'last node per level' problems and works naturally with the levelSize trick from M07 L3; DFS is more CONCISE (no queue, no levelSize tracking) and generalizes elegantly to any 'first visit per depth' variant; for interviews, BFS is often clearer to explain conceptually ('last node at each level'), while DFS code is shorter; both are O(n) time and O(n) space
DFS is always O(log n); BFS is O(n), making DFS strictly preferable
They cannot both be used; only one approach is algorithmically valid
theory_mcq.explanation: The lesson explicitly covers both: 'BFS approach: last node per level' (intuitive, leverages existing BFS level-order knowledge) vs 'DFS approach: right subtree first, track max depth seen' (concise, elegant depth-tracking trick) — both achieve identical results and complexity, so the choice is often about clarity in context.

logic_mcq.question: Trace the DFS right side view on the tree [1,(2,null,5),(3,null,4)]. What happens at node 2 (depth=1), and why is it NOT added to the result?
options: Node 2 is added to the result because it has a child

At depth=1, the DFS visits node 3 FIRST (right subtree of root 1) — since depth=1 equals result.length=1 (only [1] recorded so far), node 3 is added (result=[1,3]); when DFS then visits node 2 (also depth=1), depth=1 < result.length=2 — the condition `depth === result.length` is FALSE — so node 2 is NOT added; node 2 is blocked from the right side view by node 3 which is to its right
Node 2 is not visited at all by the DFS
Node 2 is added to result but then removed later
logic_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's DFS trace: 'right=3:depth=1 result=[1,3]... left=2:depth=1 result.length=2!=1 skip' — the right-first DFS ensures node 3 always claims depth=1 before node 2 gets a chance, correctly implementing the 'rightmost visible' semantics.

logic_mcq.question: For the same tree [1,(2,null,5),(3,null,4)], verify: what does `rightSideViewBFS` return, and what does `rightSideViewDFS` return?

Both return [1,3,4] — BFS sees level0=[1], level1=[2,3] (last=3), level2=[5,4] (last=4); DFS goes right-first: depth0→1 (add 1), depth1→3 (add 3), depth2→4 (add 4), then visits left subtree nodes 2 and 5 which find their depths already recorded — both implementations agree on [1,3,4]

lessons.explanation: Count Good Nodes (LeetCode #1448) defines a good node as one where no value on the path from the root to that node is strictly greater than the node's value. In other words, the node's value is >= the maximum value seen so far on the path from root. The solution uses top-down DFS where we pass the running maximum down through recursive calls. At each node: check if node.val >= maxSoFar (if yes, this node is good). Update maxSoFar = max(maxSoFar, node.val) before recursing into children. Count good nodes using either a closure variable or by returning the count from each recursive call and summing. This problem is a canonical example of the top-down DFS pattern: information (the running path maximum) flows downward from root to leaves, and counting flows upward on return. The root is always good (no ancestors).
lessons.analogy: Count Good Nodes is like counting employees who are the highest earner on their chain of command from CEO down to them. You start at the CEO (root) noting their salary (maxSoFar). lessons.title: Serialize And Deserialize Binary Tree
lessons.objective: Implement serialize and deserialize for a binary tree using preorder DFS with null markers, and understand why this encoding is complete, unique, and efficiently reconstructable.
concepts: Serialization: convert tree to string representation
Deserialization: reconstruct tree from string
Preorder DFS with null markers: complete and lossless encoding
Why level-order encoding is also valid but more complex
String format: 'val,val,null,null,...'
Queue-based deserializer: consume values in preorder
Why inorder alone is insufficient: multiple trees share same inorder
Codec class: encode and decode methods
lessons.explanation: Serialization converts a binary tree to a string so it can be stored or transmitted, and deserialization reconstructs the tree from the string. The preorder DFS approach with null markers is the cleanest. Serialize: do preorder DFS, appending each node's value to a list. When a null is encountered, append 'null'. Join the list with commas. Deserialize: split the string by commas into a queue of values. Use a recursive function: dequeue the next value. If it is 'null', return null (this subtree is empty). Otherwise create a node with that value, recurse for the left child, recurse for the right child. This works because the preorder with null markers uniquely encodes any binary tree — the null markers tell the deserializer exactly where subtrees end. Without null markers, the preorder sequence alone is ambiguous between multiple different tree structures.
lessons.analogy: Serialize with null markers is like writing a map of a building where every room has two doors (left and right). You walk through the building depth-first, writing down each room number. When you open a door and find a wall (null), you write 'WALL'. Anyone with your written list can reconstruct the exact building layout by following the same walking order and building rooms or walls as they read each entry.

code_example.explanation: The index pointer i shared across all recursive build() calls is the key to the deserialization. Each call to build() consumes exactly the right number of tokens for the subtree it is building — a leaf consumes 3 tokens (its value + 2 nulls), an internal node consumes its own token plus whatever its left and right subtrees consume. The pointer advances naturally through the preorder sequence.

common_mistakes: Using a class-level index or global variable for the deserializer pointer instead of a closure — if the deserializer is called multiple times, a global index carries over from the previous call; use a local index or a mutable object wrapper

Forgetting that each null leaf consumes one token — every null in the tree is represented by 'null' in the serialized string; the total number of tokens equals 2n+1 where n is the number of nodes (each node contributes its value plus eventually two null markers for empty children)

Thinking inorder serialization would also work — inorder traversal without null markers is not unique: [1,2,3] and [3,2,1] can produce the same inorder output with different structures; null markers are required for inorder too, making it no simpler than preorder

It tests understanding of tree structure encoding, not just traversal. The question 'why is null marking necessary?' and 'what would happen without null markers?' are specific follow-ups interviewers use to probe depth of understanding.

flashcards.back: Preorder records root first, making reconstruction unambiguous. Null markers encode tree structure (where subtrees end) so no separate structure info is needed. Unique encoding for every tree.

flashcards.front: How many tokens does serialization produce for a tree with n nodes?

Total = n values + (n+1) nulls = 2n+1.

flashcards.front: Why does inorder serialization alone fail?
flashcards.back: Multiple different trees can produce identical inorder sequences. Example: [1,2] can be root=1,right=2 OR root=2,left=1. Without structure info (null markers), inorder is ambiguous.

flashcards.front: Deserialization: how does the index pointer advance correctly?
flashcards.back: Each recursive build() call consumes exactly the tokens for its subtree: its own value + left subtree tokens + right subtree tokens. The pointer naturally advances through the preorder sequence without any manual tracking.

flashcards.front: How does BFS serialization differ from preorder DFS?
flashcards.back: BFS encodes level by level (like [1,2,3,null,null,4,5]). Better for balanced trees (shorter strings), worse for skewed trees. Deserialization requires careful index arithmetic for parent-child relationships.

Without null markers, multiple structurally different trees can produce IDENTICAL traversal sequences (e.g., a tree with value 1 and left child 2 vs a tree with values 1 and 2 but 2 as right child both produce preorder [1,2] without nulls); inorder alone is insufficient because the same inorder sequence can correspond to multiple different tree structures — null markers in preorder uniquely identify both the structure and values simultaneously

theory_mcq.question: In `deserialize`, why does the `build()` function use a CLOSURE VARIABLE `i` (an index into the vals array) rather than passing `i` as a parameter?
options: Passing i as a parameter would produce identical behavior — the choice is stylistic

The index `i` must PERSIST and ADVANCE ACROSS recursive calls — when `build()` processes a subtree and returns, the parent's call needs to continue from where the subtree's deserialization stopped; a parameter would create a LOCAL copy of i at each call level that doesn't propagate back to the parent after the callee advances it; a shared closure variable correctly maintains a single advancing pointer across the entire deserialization process
JavaScript does not support passing integers as parameters to recursive functions
The index i is always 0 at the start of each build() call
theory_mcq.explanation: The shared `i` variable is the critical mechanism: as build() recursively constructs the left subtree (consuming several tokens), `i` advances past all those tokens; when the parent call then invokes build() for the right subtree, `i` starts exactly at the first token belonging to the right subtree — this sequential consumption requires a shared mutable index, not a per-call copy.

logic_mcq.question: For the tree [1,(2),(3,4,5)], what is the exact serialized string, and trace the first three tokens consumed during deserialization?

Serialized: '1,2,null,null,3,4,null,null,5,null,null' — confirmed by direct execution; deserialization: token '1' → create node(1), token '2' → create node(2) as left child, token 'null' → null (node 2's left child), then another 'null' → null (node 2's right child), returning node(2) complete; then token '3' → create node(3) as right child of 1
Serialized: '1,2,3,null,null,4,5,null,null,null,null'
Deserialization consumes tokens in reverse order from the end
logic_mcq.explanation: Confirmed by direct execution: serialize returns exactly '1,2,null,null,3,4,null,null,5,null,null' matching the lesson's console.log; deserialization consumes preorder tokens sequentially — node 1, then node 2 (with its two null children), then node 3 (with nodes 4 and 5 as children each with two null children).

logic_mcq.question: Why does preorder (root→left→right) work well for this serialization scheme, while other traversal orders would be more complex to deserialize?
options: All traversal orders are equally easy to deserialize

Preorder produces the ROOT value FIRST — when deserializing, the first token is immediately the current node's value, then the left subtree tokens, then the right subtree tokens, naturally matching the recursive build() structure; inorder interleaves root between children (making it hard to know where left subtree ends and root begins without additional markers), and level-order requires tracking which level each node belongs to, making reconstruction more complex
Preorder is the only order that includes null markers
Postorder would be equally simple; preorder is chosen only by convention
logic_mcq.explanation: Preorder's root-first property aligns perfectly with the top-down tree construction process: the first token is always the current node's value, and the null markers for child positions appear immediately after the subtree they terminate — this makes the recursive build() structure a direct mirror of the serialization's recursive structure.

syntax_mcq.question: In `deserialize`, `const node = new TreeNode(Number(vals[i++]))` uses `vals[i++]`. What does the post-increment `i++` accomplish here?
options: i++ increments i BEFORE reading vals[i], so it reads the next token

i++ is a post-increment: it reads `vals[i]` FIRST (using the CURRENT value of i), then increments i for subsequent reads — this correctly reads the current token as the node's value and simultaneously advances the index to point to the next token, which will be the first token of the left subtree; the same pattern appears in the null check (`if (vals[i] === 'null') { i++; return null; }`)
i++ and ++i are interchangeable in all JavaScript contexts

lessons.title: Binary Tree Maximum Path Sum
lessons.objective: Find the maximum sum path in a binary tree in O(n) using the same single-pass postorder pattern as Diameter, returning the best one-sided gain while updating a global maximum.
concepts: Path definition: any sequence of nodes connected by edges, no node repeated
A path can start and end at any nodes (not just root to leaf)
Maximum gain from a node: max(0, best one-sided path through this node)
Why gain is clamped to 0: negative subtrees are excluded
Path through a node: node.val + leftGain + rightGain
Return only one side: parent can extend in only one direction
Closure variable tracks global max across all nodes
Connection to Diameter: same pattern, values instead of heights
lessons.explanation: Binary Tree Maximum Path Sum asks for the maximum sum of any path in the tree, where a path is any sequence of connected nodes and each node appears at most once. This is the value-sum version of the Diameter problem from Module 7. The key insight: define gain(node) as the maximum sum achievable starting at node and going downward in one direction. At a leaf, gain = max(0, leaf.val) (0 if negative, exclude the subtree). At an internal node, gain = node.val + max(0, gain(left), gain(right)) — take the better side or neither if both are negative. The maximum path passing through node = node.val + max(0, gain(left)) + max(0, gain(right)) — both sides can be included for a path through this node, but only one side can be returned to the parent (a path going left, through the node, and right cannot be extended further upward without revisiting the node). Track the global maximum across all nodes using a closure variable.
lessons.analogy: Maximum Path Sum is like finding the most profitable trade route through a network of cities where some cities have toll costs (negative values). At each city, you decide: is it worth going through my left or right region? If the profit from a region is negative, skip it entirely (clamp to 0). The best route through any given city uses the most profitable region on each side. But you can only report one direction back to the city that connected you — you cannot go both ways and still continue upward.

code_example.explanation: Initialising globalMax to -Infinity (not 0) handles the case where all nodes have negative values. The answer for an all-negative tree is the single least-negative node. Using 0 as the initial globalMax would incorrectly return 0 (an empty path), but the problem defines a path as having at least one node.

common_mistakes: Returning node.val + leftGain + rightGain from the gain function instead of node.val + max(leftGain, rightGain) — the gain function must return the best one-sided extension for the parent; returning both sides would mean the path goes left through this node and right through this node, which cannot be extended by the parent without revisiting this node
Initialising globalMax to 0 — fails for all-negative trees where the answer is negative; initialise to -Infinity

Not clamping gains to 0 with Math.max(0, gain(child)) — without clamping, including a negative-sum subtree would decrease the total; the max(0, ...) ensures we never include a subtree that hurts the sum

theory_mcq.question: Why does the `gain` function clamp contributions to `Math.max(0, gain(child))` rather than taking the raw gain, even when a subtree's gain might be negative?
options: Clamping to 0 excludes all leaf nodes from the path

A negative subtree gain would DECREASE the overall path sum — if the best path through a node's left subtree has a negative sum, it's better to NOT include that subtree in the path (contributing 0 instead of a negative amount); clamping to max(0, gain) effectively treats a negative-gain subtree as 'not included', since any path that would include a negative subtree would have a higher sum by stopping at the current node instead
Clamping is required to prevent integer overflow
Math.max(0, gain) is equivalent to Math.abs(gain) in this context
theory_mcq.explanation: The clamping is the core optimization: if a subtree only contributes a negative amount to any path through it, it's better to exclude it entirely (contribute 0) — this allows the algorithm to find the maximum sum path without being dragged down by negative subtrees, while still correctly finding the maximum in all-negative trees through the globalMax initialization to -Infinity.

theory_mcq.question: Why does `gain(node)` return `node.val + Math.max(leftGain, rightGain)` (one-sided) to its parent, rather than `node.val + leftGain + rightGain` (both-sided)?
options: Both are equivalent; the distinction has no effect

A path in a tree cannot BRANCH — once a path goes from a parent to a child, it must continue in ONE direction from that child (it cannot go to the child and then split both left and right simultaneously); the parent can EXTEND the current path by including only ONE of the child's branches; the two-sided sum (node.val + leftGain + rightGain) IS computed for the global maximum update (path ending at this node using both branches), but only one side is returned to the parent since the parent can only extend in one direction
Math.max is used because leftGain and rightGain are always equal
Returning both sides would cause the function to visit nodes twice
theory_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's explicit concept: 'Return only one side: parent can extend in only one direction' — a tree path has no branching, so the contribution a child can offer to its parent is limited to the best single-directional extension; the both-sided sum (for the globalMax) and the one-sided return (for the parent) serve different purposes in the same function.

logic_mcq.question: Why does `globalMax` initialize to `-Infinity` rather than `0`, and what would go wrong if initialized to 0 for an all-negative tree like [-3]?
options: Initializing to 0 works correctly for all trees including all-negative ones

For a tree containing only negative values (like [-3]), every valid path sum is negative — if globalMax were initialized to 0, the function would return 0 (implying an 'empty path' with sum 0), which is incorrect since the problem requires at least one node; initializing to -Infinity ensures the ACTUAL maximum over all valid (non-empty) paths is found, even when that maximum is negative
Initializing to -Infinity prevents the function from handling empty trees
globalMax initialization doesn't affect the final result for any tree

Answer: -3 (single node is the path)'.

syntax_mcq.question: In `maxPathSum`, `globalMax` is declared with `let` in the outer function scope and updated inside the inner `gain` function via closure. How does this differ from the return-based aggregation approach used in `goodNodes`?
options: They are identical; both use return-based aggregation

goodNodes returns an INTEGER COUNT from each call and adds them (the answer decomposes naturally as a sum of per-node counts); maxPathSum cannot use return-based aggregation because `gain` must return the ONE-SIDED gain to the parent for its own path computation — if gain returned the global max instead, the parent would have no way to extend the path; the closure variable lets the global max be tracked SEPARATELY from the per-node return value, allowing both to coexist
The closure approach is always slower than return-based aggregation
goodNodes also uses a closure variable; the lesson's code contains an error
syntax_mcq.explanation: This is the same design trade-off as diameter vs goodNodes: diameter and maxPathSum need to return LOCAL information (height/one-sided gain) to parents while ALSO tracking a GLOBAL maximum — the two needs are incompatible with a single return value, requiring the closure variable; goodNodes' answer (total count) decomposes cleanly as a sum, making return-based aggregation sufficient.

lessons.title: Kth Smallest In BST
lessons.objective: Find the kth smallest element in a BST in O(h+k) using inorder traversal with early termination, and implement an iterator-based approach for repeated queries.
concepts: Inorder traversal of BST produces sorted ascending sequence
kth smallest = kth element in inorder traversal
Recursive inorder with counter: return early when k reaches 0
O(h+k) time: h to reach leftmost node, k to count up
O(h) space: call stack depth
Iterative inorder using explicit stack: avoids recursion limit
BST iterator pattern: hasNext and next in O(h) amortized
Augmented BST: store subtree size for O(log n) kth smallest
lessons.explanation: The kth smallest element in a BST is the kth element produced by an inorder traversal, since inorder visits BST nodes in ascending sorted order. The recursive approach: perform inorder traversal, decrement a counter k at each visited node, return the node's value when k reaches 0. The O(h+k) complexity comes from: O(h) to traverse down to the leftmost leaf, then O(k) to count back up to the kth node. An iterative approach using an explicit stack simulates the call stack and allows early termination more naturally. For the BST iterator (LeetCode #173), maintaining a stack that holds the current path from root to the next unprocessed node gives O(h) amortized time per next() call and O(h) space at any time — only the current path is in the stack, not the entire left subtree.
lessons.analogy: Kth smallest in BST is like reading the kth word in a dictionary. The dictionary is sorted (BST inorder = sorted). You page through from the beginning until you reach the kth word. You do not need to read the whole dictionary — stop as soon as you hit the kth word. The BST iterator is like a bookmark: it remembers where you last stopped so you can resume without restarting from page 1.

code_example.explanation: The BSTIterator's _pushLeft method pushes the entire leftmost path from a given node. On next(), the top of the stack is the smallest unvisited node. After returning it, we push the leftmost path of its right subtree. This lazy evaluation means we only push paths we will actually need, keeping space at O(h) rather than O(n).

common_mistakes: Not implementing early exit in the recursive approach — without the result !== null guard, the recursion continues visiting nodes after finding the kth element, wasting O(n-k) additional work
Counting nodes in a simple counter variable without early exit and then iterating the full inorder — this gives O(n) time; the early exit makes it O(h+k)

Not understanding the BSTIterator's amortized O(h) claim — a single next() call might push O(h) nodes onto the stack, making it look like O(h) per call; but each node is pushed and popped at most once across all calls, so the total work across n calls is O(n+h) = O(n), giving O(1) amortized, or O(h) if considering only the push work
lessons.interview_relevance: Kth Smallest Element in BST (#230) is Blind 75. BST Iterator (#173) is Blind 75. Both are directly solvable with inorder traversal knowledge from Module 7 applied with an early exit optimisation. Knowing the BST iterator pattern is specifically asked at companies that build search or database products where repeated ordered iteration is a common operation.

Two cases: (1) p has a right subtree: the answer is the leftmost node of the right subtree. (2) p has no right subtree: the answer is the lowest ancestor for which p is in its left subtree.

The complexity is O(k log n) because k nodes each take O(log n) to find

Post-decrement is preferred here and pre-decrement is the error

lessons.title: Trie Data Structure — Insert And Search
lessons.objective: Implement a Trie from scratch with insert, search, and startsWith in O(m) per operation, and understand why Tries outperform hash maps for prefix-based queries.
concepts: Trie definition: tree where each path from root to a node spells a prefix
TrieNode: children map (or array of 26) + isEnd flag
Insert: create nodes along the character path, mark isEnd
Search: follow character path, check isEnd at last character
StartsWith (prefix search): follow character path, return true if reachable
O(m) per operation where m = word length
Space: O(ALPHABET_SIZE * m * n) for n words of average length m
Trie vs hash map: O(m) both, but Trie supports prefix queries natively
lessons.explanation: A Trie (prefix tree) is a tree data structure where each node represents a character, and the path from the root to any node spells out a prefix of words stored in the Trie. Each TrieNode has up to 26 children (for lowercase English letters) stored in a Map or fixed-size array, plus an isEnd boolean flag marking whether the path to this node spells a complete word. Insert: start at root, for each character in the word, go to (or create) the corresponding child node. After processing all characters, set the last node's isEnd to true. Search: follow the same path as insert. If any character's child does not exist, the word is not in the Trie. At the end, the word is present only if the last node's isEnd is true. StartsWith: same as search but do not check isEnd at the end — any reachable path is a valid prefix. Tries give O(m) time for all three operations (m = word length) and O(1) prefix matching that a hash map cannot provide — a hash map requires a separate entry for every possible prefix, while a Trie shares prefixes by construction.
lessons.analogy: A Trie is like an autocomplete index card system. The filing cabinet has 26 drawers for each letter. 'apple' creates a path: drawer A → drawer P → drawer P → drawer L → drawer E, with a red dot on the last card meaning 'complete word here'. Searching for 'app' just walks the first three drawers and returns true because the path exists. Searching for 'app' as a complete word would fail because drawer P (third) has no red dot. A hash map would need a separate card for 'a', 'ap', 'app', 'appl', 'apple' — five cards instead of sharing the path.

code_example.explanation: The Map-based children is more memory-efficient when the character set is large or words use only a small subset of characters. The Array-based children is faster due to O(1) direct index access vs O(1) hash map access (with lower constant). For competitive programming or memory-critical applications, the Array-based version is standard. For interview solutions, either is acceptable.

common_mistakes: Returning true at the end of search without checking isEnd — the path to 'appl' exists in a Trie containing 'apple', but 'appl' is not a complete word; always check isEnd for exact word search
Not initialising the root node before operations — the root is a TrieNode with no character value, it simply serves as the starting point; every insert and search starts from root
Confusing search and startsWith — search checks isEnd at the final character; startsWith does not check isEnd, it only verifies the path exists
lessons.interview_relevance: Implement Trie (#208) is Blind 75. It is asked at every company that has autocomplete, search, or dictionary features in their product. Being able to implement the Trie class from scratch in under 10 minutes and explain the O(m) operations and the search vs startsWith distinction is a clear signal of data structure depth.
lessons.mini_challenge: Implement the Trie class above. Then add a delete(word) method that removes a word from the Trie. Deletion must handle three cases: (1) word not in trie (do nothing), (2) word is a prefix of another word (just unset isEnd), (3) word has no children after deletion (remove the nodes to save space). Finally, implement countWordsWithPrefix(prefix): return the number of words in the trie that start with the given prefix. This requires either storing a count at each node or doing a DFS from the prefix endpoint.

flashcards.back: Trie shares prefixes structurally — 'apple', 'app', 'application' all share the same a→p→p path. Hash map needs a separate entry for each word. Prefix check in Trie = O(m); in hash map = check each possible prefix separately.

theory_mcq.question: What is a Trie structurally, and why does each operation (`insert`, `search`, `startsWith`) take O(m) time where m is the word/prefix length?
options: A Trie is a hash map where keys are full words; operations are O(1)

A Trie is a tree where each PATH from root to a node spells a PREFIX — characters are stored on edges (represented by children map keys), and each node represents the prefix formed by following the root-to-node path; insert/search/startsWith all take O(m) because they traverse EXACTLY m character links (one per character in the word/prefix) regardless of how many words are stored, making them independent of the vocabulary size n
Trie operations are O(m log n) because the children map uses binary search
O(m) only applies to search; insert is O(m * ALPHABET_SIZE)
theory_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's explicit complexity: 'O(m) per operation where m = word length' — traversing the character path involves exactly m steps (one per character), and each step is O(1) with a HashMap (or O(1) with a direct-indexed array), making all three core operations O(m) independent of the total number of stored words.

theory_mcq.question: What is the critical difference between `search(word)` and `startsWith(prefix)`, and why does `search` require checking `node.isEnd` while `startsWith` does not?
options: Both check isEnd; startsWith is just a shorthand for search

`search` requires that the traversed character path corresponds to a COMPLETE WORD that was inserted (the path must end at a node marked isEnd=true) — without isEnd, 'appl' would falsely match as a word when only 'apple' was inserted; `startsWith` only requires the prefix PATH to EXIST in the Trie (any reachable node is a valid prefix endpoint) — it doesn't matter whether a complete word ends at that node
startsWith is more expensive because it doesn't check isEnd
isEnd is only relevant when a Trie stores words with duplicate prefixes
theory_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's exact test: `trie.search('appl') // false (isEnd=false for 'appl')` vs `trie.startsWith('appl') // true (prefix exists)` — the isEnd flag distinguishes 'prefix of a stored word' from 'complete stored word'; startsWith only needs reachability while search requires both reachability AND isEnd=true at the final character.

logic_mcq.question: After inserting 'apple', 'app', and 'application' into a Trie, what are the `isEnd` values for nodes reachable by the prefix 'app', 'appl', and 'apple'?
options: All three have isEnd=true since all share the prefix 'app'

Node at 'app' (end of 'app'): isEnd=true (word 'app' was inserted); node at 'appl' (after 'app'+'l'): isEnd=false (no word 'appl' was inserted); node at 'apple' (end of 'apple'): isEnd=true (word 'apple' was inserted) — confirmed by direct execution: `trie.search('app')=true`, `trie.search('appl')=false`, `trie.search('apple')=true`
isEnd is only true at the final node of the longest inserted word
Only 'application' has isEnd=true; shorter prefixes are never marked
logic_mcq.explanation: Confirmed by direct execution matching the lesson's console.log outputs: isEnd is set at the EXACT position where `insert` terminates for each word — 'app' marks the 'p' node (position 3) as isEnd=true, 'apple' marks a different later 'e' node as isEnd=true, but nodes representing mere prefixes like 'appl' remain isEnd=false.

logic_mcq.question: What is the trade-off between the Map-based `TrieNode` and the array-based `TrieNodeArray` (26 slots)?
options: Array-based is always strictly better in every dimension

Array-based (26 fixed slots): O(1) character access via index (no hashing), better cache locality, no hash overhead — but WASTES memory for sparse alphabets (26 null slots even for nodes with 1-2 children); Map-based: memory-proportional (only stores actual children), works for any character set (Unicode, mixed case), but slightly higher overhead per access due to Map internals
Map-based is always better because Maps automatically sort their keys
Array-based can only be used for uppercase letters; Map works for all cases
logic_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's explicit contrast: 'Faster access: children[char.charCodeAt(0) - 97]. No hash overhead, cache-friendly, but 26 slots even if mostly null' — the array trades memory for speed, useful for lowercase-English-only problems; the Map trades speed for memory and flexibility, supporting arbitrary character sets.

syntax_mcq.question: In `insert`, why does the traversal loop use `for (const char of word)` rather than a traditional `for (let i = 0; i < word.length; i++)`?
options: Traditional for-loops cannot access string characters

Both are functionally equivalent for ASCII strings; `for...of` is preferred here for READABILITY — it iterates characters directly without index arithmetic, making the intent ('process each character') clearer; the character variable `char` is immediately usable without `word[i]` dereferencing; for Unicode strings with multi-byte characters, `for...of` is also SAFER as it correctly handles surrogate pairs that index-based access can split
for...of automatically filters out non-alphabetic characters
Traditional for-loops are O(n²) for string character access; for...of is O(n)
syntax_mcq.explanation: Both approaches work identically for ASCII/single-byte strings; `for...of` is idiomatic JavaScript for character-by-character string iteration, producing cleaner code that directly names each character rather than using index notation — the lesson uses this consistent pattern across all three Trie methods.

DFS from prefix endpoint: traverse all paths to isEnd nodes
Wildcard search: '.' matches any character

Design Add and Search Words Data Structure (LeetCode #211)

Longest word with all prefixes in dictionary: isEnd check at every character

lessons.explanation: Autocomplete extends the Trie with a collect operation: after navigating to the endpoint of a prefix, do a DFS of the entire subtree collecting all paths that end at an isEnd node. Each complete path from root to an isEnd node represents a word. The DFS appends characters as it descends and removes them on backtrack, building the word character by character. Wildcard search handles the '.' character that matches any child. When processing a '.' in the search string, iterate over all children of the current node and recurse into each one. This DFS with branching is correct but expensive for strings with many wildcards: O(ALPHABET_SIZE^wildcards) in the worst case. Design Add and Search Words Data Structure (LeetCode #211) implements exactly this: addWord inserts into a Trie, search handles '.' wildcards via recursive DFS.
lessons.analogy: Autocomplete DFS is like a librarian who walks all the aisles starting from a certain shelf (prefix endpoint) and writes down the title of every book they find (isEnd nodes). Wildcard search is like the librarian searching for a book title pattern like 'c.t' — they must check every book starting with 'c' and ending with 't' because '.' could be any letter. One wildcard is manageable; many wildcards mean checking almost everything.

code_example.explanation: The wildcard _dfs iterates over all children of the current node when it encounters '.'. The for loop short-circuits with return true as soon as any path succeeds, avoiding unnecessary work. In the worst case (all wildcards, large dictionary), this degrades to O(n) where n is the total number of characters in the dictionary, since it may visit every node.

common_mistakes: Not handling '.' by iterating all children — a common mistake is to check only if the current character exists; for '.', every existing child must be explored
Returning false immediately after the wildcard loop without trying all children — the loop must try every child before returning false; returning false inside the loop (not after it) exits too early
Forgetting to check isEnd at the end of the search string in _dfs — when i === word.length, the path has been followed completely; only return true if the current node marks a complete word (isEnd)

theory_mcq.question: In `getWordsWithPrefix`, why is DFS used to collect words after navigating to the prefix endpoint, rather than any other traversal?
options: BFS would work identically for word collection

After navigating to the prefix endpoint, all COMPLETE WORDS are scattered throughout the SUBTREE below that node — they're at nodes marked isEnd=true at various depths; DFS naturally explores all paths in this subtree, and the `if (curr.isEnd)` check can record a complete word whenever one is encountered; BFS would also work but DFS is simpler here since we're collecting ALL paths to isEnd nodes rather than just the shallowest ones
DFS is required because the Trie stores words in DFS order
Only DFS can traverse a Map-based TrieNode's children
theory_mcq.explanation: DFS is the natural choice for exhaustive path exploration in a subtree — it visits every node reachable from the prefix endpoint, recording the path word whenever isEnd=true is encountered; the lesson's implementation builds the current word by concatenating characters as it descends, and records complete words at isEnd=true nodes.

theory_mcq.question: In `WordDictionary`, what makes the wildcard '.' character fundamentally different to handle compared to exact characters, and why does it require iterating ALL children?
options: The '.' character is only special at the end of a word

An exact character has ONE matching child (or none, causing immediate failure); a '.' matches ANY character, meaning it could correspond to ANY of the current node's children — there's no way to narrow down which child to follow without trying all of them; this is why the `_dfs` function iterates `node.children.values()` for '.', attempting each child and returning true if ANY one succeeds (backtracking if one fails)

Wildcard '.' matches only nodes where isEnd=true
theory_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's code: `for (const child of node.children.values()) { if (this._dfs(child, word, i+1)) return true; }` — since '.' could represent any of the 26 possible characters, ALL children must be explored (backtracking DFS), vs exact characters where exactly zero or one child is relevant.

None of the children are tried for '.' because it matches everything automatically
_dfs tries all three children but none match because the pattern is ambiguous
logic_mcq.explanation: Confirmed by direct execution: `.ad` matches 'bad', 'dad', and 'mad' — _dfs tries ALL root children for '.'; the first one tried ('b' subtree, which contains 'bad') succeeds (returns true at i=3 with isEnd=true), causing the function to return true immediately without trying 'd' or 'm' subtrees.

When all characters are consumed (i === word.length), the function must verify that the current node actually represents a COMPLETE WORD end — returning `node.isEnd` returns true only if a word was inserted ending at exactly this node, and false if the consumed path represents only a prefix of a longer word; returning `true` unconditionally would incorrectly match prefixes as complete words (e.g., searching 'ba' would return true even if only 'bad' was inserted)
node.isEnd can be null, not just true/false
The return type must be boolean for the wildcard branch to work correctly

lessons.title: Word Search II Using Trie
lessons.objective: Solve Word Search II in O(m*n*4^L) using a Trie combined with backtracking DFS on a 2D grid, and apply the pruning optimisation that removes matched words from the Trie.
concepts: Word Search II: find all words from a list that exist in a 2D character grid
Naive approach: run Word Search I for each word separately O(W*m*n*4^L)
Trie optimisation: share prefix matching across all words simultaneously
DFS on grid: 4-directional backtracking with visited marking
Pruning: remove matched words from Trie to avoid duplicate results
Pruning: remove empty nodes after word removal to speed up future searches
Time: O(m*n*4^L) where L = length of longest word
Connection: Trie provides O(1) prefix validity check during grid DFS
lessons.explanation: Word Search II requires finding all words from a given list that exist as paths in a 2D character grid. The naive approach runs the Word Search I DFS separately for each word: O(W * m*n * 4^L) total. With a Trie, all words are searched simultaneously in one grid traversal: insert all words into a Trie, then start a DFS from every cell in the grid. At each DFS step, check if the current character exists as a child in the Trie node. If not, prune the search. If yes, continue the DFS following the Trie node. When a Trie node with isEnd=true is reached, the current path spells a complete word — add it to results. This reduces redundant work because all words sharing a common prefix share the same Trie traversal path. Two important pruning optimisations: (1) Remove found words from the Trie to avoid adding them to results multiple times. (2) Remove leaf nodes with no children after word removal to keep the Trie small and reduce future search overhead.
lessons.analogy: Word Search II with a Trie is like a search party looking for multiple missing persons simultaneously. Instead of each searcher looking for one person separately (naive), all searchers share a map (Trie) showing all possible name prefixes. As they traverse the forest (grid), they use the map to know immediately whether the path they are on could lead to any person's name. If the current path prefix matches nothing on the map, they stop immediately without exploring further.

code_example.explanation: Storing the word string in isEnd (instead of a boolean) allows direct retrieval when a word is found without maintaining a separate path string. Setting isEnd = false after finding a word prevents duplicates without rebuilding the Trie. The leaf pruning (delete char from parent when nextNode.children.size === 0) progressively shrinks the Trie, making subsequent searches faster.

common_mistakes: Not marking cells as visited during the DFS — without the board[row][col] = '#' marking, the same cell can be used multiple times in one path, incorrectly forming words that use a cell more than once
Forgetting to restore the cell after backtracking — without board[row][col] = char after the DFS, the board is permanently modified and subsequent searches from other starting cells fail

Not implementing the pruning optimisations — without word removal and leaf pruning, the solution passes all test cases but times out on large inputs; the Trie grows stale and continues matching already-found words
lessons.interview_relevance: Word Search II (#212) is Blind 75 and consistently rated as one of the hardest Blind 75 problems. It combines two hard topics (Trie and backtracking DFS on a grid) and requires both the core algorithm and the pruning optimisations to pass within time limits. Being able to explain why Trie reduces the naive O(W * m*n * 4^L) to O(m*n * 4^L) and articulate both pruning optimisations is a senior-level signal.

flashcards.front: Word Search II: why does Trie beat the naive per-word approach?
flashcards.back: Naive: O(W × m×n × 4^L) — runs Word Search I separately for each of W words. Trie: O(m×n × 4^L) — all words searched simultaneously. Shared prefixes are explored once, not W times.

flashcards.front: How is visited marking done in Word Search II?
flashcards.back: In-place: board[row][col] = '#' before recursing (marks as visited). Restore board[row][col] = char after recursing (backtrack). No separate visited set needed — saves O(m×n) space.

flashcards.front: Pruning optimisation 1: word removal?
flashcards.back: After finding a word, set nextNode.isEnd = false (or null). Prevents adding the same word to results multiple times if its path appears again.

flashcards.front: Pruning optimisation 2: leaf node removal?
flashcards.back: After DFS from a Trie node, if nextNode.children.size === 0, delete it from the parent's children map. Progressively shrinks the Trie, reducing future search overhead.

flashcards.front: Why store the word string in isEnd instead of a boolean?
flashcards.back: When a match is found, result.push(nextNode.isEnd) directly gives the word without maintaining a separate current-path string. Simpler code, same O(L) space.

flashcards.front: Time complexity of Word Search II?
flashcards.back: O(m×n × 4^L) where m×n = grid cells and L = longest word length. The Trie prefix check prunes invalid paths early — shared prefix traversals are not repeated.

quiz.question: Why must board[row][col] be restored after DFS in Word Search II?

Restoration is optional — '#' marks are harmless
To avoid modifying a const array
quiz.explanation: Without restoration, a cell marked '#' during one DFS path would be permanently unavailable for DFS paths starting from other cells, causing missed words.

quiz.question: After finding word 'oath', what does the pruning do to the Trie?
options: Deletes the entire Trie and rebuilds
Sets isEnd=false at the 'h' node so 'oath' isn't added again
Removes the 'o' subtree entirely
Nothing — pruning only affects performance, not correctness
quiz.explanation: Pruning 1: nextNode.isEnd = false prevents duplicate results. Pruning 2 (leaf removal) may also trim dead branches but only after DFS completes from that node.

quiz.question: The Trie prefix check prunes invalid DFS paths by?
options: Stopping DFS when current character has no matching Trie child
Marking all visited cells as invalid
Reversing the word list
Using BFS instead of DFS
quiz.explanation: If board[row][col] has no child in the current Trie node, no word in the dictionary can be formed along this path. Return immediately — no further DFS needed.

visual_aid.diagram:
Step 1: Build Trie from word list

theory_mcq.question: Why does using a Trie for Word Search II outperform running Word Search I separately for each word in the list?
options: A Trie is slower; running Word Search I per word is always faster

Running Word Search I separately for W words costs O(W * m * n * 4^L); a Trie allows all W words' prefix trees to be SEARCHED SIMULTANEOUSLY during a single DFS pass — when DFS reaches a cell, a single Trie lookup checks if ANY word's prefix continues through this character, rather than repeating the entire DFS for each word independently; shared prefix work is done ONCE instead of W times
The Trie approach only helps when all words have the same length
Word Search II with Trie is O(1); single-word searches are O(n)
theory_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's explicit analysis: 'Naive approach: run Word Search I for each word separately O(W*m*n*4^L)... Trie optimisation: share prefix matching across all words simultaneously' — the key insight is that words sharing common prefixes (e.g., 'oath' and 'oat') explore the same Trie path only once, not duplicated per word.

theory_mcq.question: The implementation stores the WORD STRING as `node.isEnd = word` (rather than just `true`). What advantage does this provide?
options: It makes no difference; true would work identically

Storing the word string as `node.isEnd` allows the algorithm to retrieve the matched word in O(1) when a Trie path terminates — instead of separately reconstructing the matched word from the grid path (which would require tracking the current path as a string or array), the word is immediately available at the Trie node; this is a common trick that avoids re-traversing the grid path for word reconstruction
isEnd must be a string for JavaScript's type system
Storing the word prevents the Trie from being reused for multiple searches
theory_mcq.explanation: Storing the word string directly in isEnd provides immediate O(1) access to the matched word when a terminal Trie node is found — `result.push(nextNode.isEnd)` directly adds the word to results, while the follow-up `nextNode.isEnd = false` efficiently prevents duplicate additions without needing a separate Set.

logic_mcq.question: In `findWords`, `board[row][col] = '#'` is used to mark a cell as visited during DFS. Why is this in-place marking preferable to maintaining a separate `visited` boolean matrix?
options: A separate matrix would be more efficient; '#' marking is an anti-pattern

In-place '#' marking uses O(1) extra space (vs O(m*n) for a separate matrix) since the board itself serves as the visited tracker; crucially, `board[row][col] = char` RESTORES the original character after DFS returns (backtracking), making the modification temporary and allowing different DFS paths from different starting cells to correctly see the board's original state
The '#' character has special meaning in the Trie that enables faster lookup
In-place marking prevents the DFS from visiting cells that are part of the Trie
logic_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's concept: 'mark visited (in-place, no extra set)' — the in-place approach saves O(m*n) space by reusing the board as the visited tracker; backtracking restoration (`board[row][col] = char`) ensures the board returns to its original state after each DFS path, allowing clean exploration from other starting cells.

logic_mcq.question: After finding a word, the code sets `nextNode.isEnd = false` and later removes empty Trie nodes. What are the two purposes served by these pruning steps?
options: Pruning is only for memory efficiency; it has no impact on correctness

Setting `isEnd = false` PREVENTS the same word from being added to results TWICE (if the word appears in the grid multiple times through different paths); removing leaf nodes (`trieNode.children.delete(char)` when `nextNode.children.size === 0`) makes subsequent DFS calls FAIL FASTER — once a subtree has no more words to find, it's entirely removed from the Trie, so future cells that lead into this defunct subtree are pruned immediately at the first character mismatch
Pruning is only required to avoid JavaScript memory limits
isEnd is set to false to allow the same word to be found again later
logic_mcq.explanation: Two distinct pruning purposes: (1) `isEnd = false` prevents duplicate word collection across multiple grid paths that both spell the same word; (2) removing empty leaf nodes shrinks the Trie during the search, accelerating subsequent DFS calls since empty branches are eliminated immediately when their last word is found.

syntax_mcq.question: In `findWords`, `if (!trieNode.children.has(char)) return;` is checked AT THE START of `dfs`. Why is this early-return critical for performance?
options: This check is redundant; the algorithm would produce identical results without it

This check implements PREFIX PRUNING — if the current grid cell's character is not a valid next character in ANY remaining word's Trie path, there's no point in exploring further from this cell in this direction; the entire subtree below this (row, col) position in this DFS path is immediately abandoned; without this check, DFS would continue exploring the 4 neighboring cells even when no word in the list could possibly be formed through this character
The check prevents the DFS from visiting the same cell twice
This check is only needed for the '#' visited marker
syntax_mcq.explanation: The Trie provides O(1) prefix validity — checking `trieNode.children.has(char)` tells whether ANY remaining search word continues through this character; a negative result means no word can be completed from this position in this DFS direction, enabling immediate backtracking and avoiding exponential unnecessary work in the O(m*n*4^L) search space.

syntax_mcq.explanation: Initializing `globalResult` inside `dfs` would reset it to its initial value at EVERY recursive call — every node invocation would start fresh rather than accumulating; placing it in the outer function scope ensures exactly ONE instance exists for the entire traversal, with all recursive calls reading and writing to the same variable through the closure mechanism.

core_patterns: LCA postorder propagation — return node-or-null, both-non-null means split point
BST LCA — exploit invariant for O(h) without full traversal
Right Side View DFS — right-first preorder, depth===result.length check
Top-down DFS — pass accumulated path state (maxSoFar, remaining, bounds) downward
Serialize preorder + null markers — 2n+1 tokens, unique encoding
Deserialize with shared index pointer — each build() consumes its subtree tokens
Max Path Sum gain() — returns one-sided, closure tracks two-sided, clamp negatives to 0
BST Iterator — _pushLeft for lazy inorder, O(h) amortized next()
Trie TrieNode — children Map + isEnd flag, O(m) all operations
Autocomplete — navigate to prefix, DFS collect all isEnd paths
Wildcard DFS — iterate all children on '.', short-circuit on first true
Word Search II — Trie + grid backtracking, in-place visited marking, both prunings
